title-group.article-title: Effects of using dextrose administration and outcome in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients with hypoglycemia during cardiopulmonary resuscitation

abstract.p: Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of cardiac arrest that can be identified during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). This study aimed to investigate the effect of prehospital intravenous (IV) dextrose administration during CPR on the outcomes of patients with OHCA with hypoglycemia compared with those without hypoglycemia who did not receive dextrose. This was a retrospective single-center cohort study including adult patients with nontraumatic OHCA aged ≥ 18 years who were assisted by Vajira Emergency Medical Service and delivered to the emergency department of the Faculty of Medicine Vajira Hospital, Navamindradhiraj University, between January 1, 2019, and June 30, 2023. Patients were divided into dextrose and nondextrose groups. The primary outcome was sustained return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) at the scene, and the secondary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Subgroup analyses were conducted by stratification according to diabetes status. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) based on propensity scores and multiple logistic regression analysis were performed for statistical evaluation. Among 246 eligible patients, sustained return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) at the scene occurred in 45.5% of the dextrose group and 44.0% of the nondextrose group, while 30-day survival was 25.6% and 12.8%, respectively. After inverse probability of treatment weighting, dextrose administration was not significantly associated with sustained ROSC at the scene (adjusted risk ratio 1.13, 95% confidence interval 0.80–1.59; p = 0.484) but was associated with a higher likelihood of 30-day survival (adjusted risk ratio 2.38, 95% confidence interval 1.18–4.80; p = 0.015). In subgroup analyses, patients with diabetes who received dextrose had markedly higher 30-day survival compared with those who did not (36.4% vs. 6.5%; adjusted risk ratio 18.86, 95% confidence interval 3.82–93.10; p < 0.001), whereas no significant benefit was observed among patients without diabetes (23.2% vs. 14.9%; adjusted risk ratio 1.81, 95% confidence interval 0.92–3.53; p = 0.084). Dextrose administration during CPR in OHCA patients with hypoglycemia was not associated with improved sustained ROSC at the scene but was linked to better survival to hospital discharge, possibly due to benefits on post-resuscitation physiology rather than immediate resuscitation success.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a major global and national public health problem, representing a leading cause of mortality and a significant medical and economic burden1. It requires urgent management in the prehospital phase by the emergency medical service (EMS) system2. The global incidence of OHCA is estimated at 28–44 per 100,000 population annually3. According to the American Heart Association (AHA), over 356,000 OHCA cases occur each year in the USA, with a mortality rate approaching 90%, and cardiovascular disease remains the most common cause of death4. In Asia, the Pan Asian Resuscitation Outcomes Study reported survival-to-discharge rates of 0.5%–8.5% and favorable neurological outcomes of 1.6%–3% after OHCA5. In Thailand, the Ministry of Public Health reported 21,870 deaths from cardiac arrest, accounting for 33.5% of all deaths, with an increasing annual trend6.
Glucose is an important energy source for cells in most living organisms7. Capillary blood glucose (CBG) level is one of the essential indicators that should be measured during cardiac arrest.

Recent evidence has highlighted the complex relationship between blood glucose levels and outcomes after OHCA. A multicenter cohort study reported that both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia on hospital arrival were significantly associated with poor outcomes, suggesting that abnormal glucose levels may influence post-resuscitation survival and neurological recovery8. These findings indicate that blood glucose disturbances are clinically relevant in OHCA, although the optimal management strategy in the prehospital phase remains uncertain9. A previous study showed that routine dextrose administration in cardiac arrest was associated with increased neurological illness and decreased survival to hospital discharge9. Another study reported that hyperglycemia following dextrose administration was associated with a decreased rate of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), prolonged recovery time, and worse neurological outcomes in patients with diabetes, reflecting the impact of chronic dysglycemia rather than acute hypoglycemia during resuscitation10. In contrast, limited evidence from case reports has suggested a potential benefit of dextrose administration in selected patients with cardiac arrest and suspected hypoglycemia11. However, these studies differ substantially in patient populations, baseline glycemic status, and clinical context. Therefore, the effect of dextrose administration specifically in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and documented hypoglycemia during cardiopulmonary resuscitation remains unclear. Although hypoglycemia is traditionally considered a potentially reversible metabolic abnormality within the H’s and T’s framework for cardiac arrest, current resuscitation guidelines do not explicitly prioritize its routine treatment during active cardiopulmonary resuscitation because of limited and inconsistent evidence.

Data on the outcomes of dextrose administration to patients with hypoglycemia during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), especially in the context of prehospital emergency care by the EMS system, are limited. Therefore, whether glucose administration during CPR in patients with OHCA with hypoglycemia can increase the rates of ROSC or survival to hospital discharge remains unclear, and more in-depth data are needed to support the AHA recommendations to improv e care for this patient population12. The present Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines in 2020 recommended the administration of dextrose with insulin to treat severe hyperkalemia and beta-blocker overdose13. However, these guidelines did not support or oppose dextrose use in other conditions. Additionally, the extent and definition of hypoglycemia were not specified standardly in the ACLS guidelines13 and considerably varied in the academic literature, which generally used a blood glucose level ≤ 70 mg/dL (3.89 mmol/L) as a cutoff value for the diagnosis of hypoglycemia14, consistent with the American Diabetes Association standard guidelines, which defined hypoglycemia as blood glucose level ≤ 70 mg/dL (< 3.9 mmol/L)15. Until now, only a few studies have investigated the effect of dextrose administration by EMS teams in fieldwork.

Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the effect of intravenous (IV) dextrose administration by EMS teams in patients with OHCA with hypoglycemia (CBG ≤ 70 mg/dL) during CPR on sustained return of spontaneous circulation (sustained ROSC) at the scene (ROSC ≥ 20 min) and survival to hospital discharge and compare between patients with OHCA with hypoglycemia who received dextrose and those without hypoglycemia who did not receive dextrose during CPR.

sec.title: Study design and setting
sec.p: This was a retrospective cohort study conducted at the Vajira Emergency Medical Service (V-EMS), an advanced life support emergency medical service unit based at the Faculty of Medicine Vajira Hospital, Navamindradhiraj University, Bangkok, Thailand. V-EMS is the leader of EMS area 1 among 11 EMS areas in Bangkok, dispatched from Erawan Center, Bangkok, and networking with six public and private hospitals in the area of responsibility16,17. V-EMS dispatches one team for each operation comprising at least three staff members, including paramedics or emergency nurse practitioners (ENPs) as an operation team leader and emergency medical technicians. During each operation, paramedics or ENPs follow offline and online medical protocols under the order of emergency physicians. In cases involving patients with cardiac arrest, the AHA guidelines are applied by paramedics or ENPs. All providers passed the Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) provider training. In accordance with the local EMS guideline of the V-EMS advanced life support protocol, point-of-care capillary blood glucose (CBG) testing was routinely performed during cardiopulmonary resuscitation to identify potentially reversible causes of cardiac arrest. If the CBG level was < 70 mg/dL, intravenous dextrose was administered immediately as part of standard prehospital care. Dextrose was given as an intravenous bolus, with a standard dose of 50 mL of 50% dextrose solution. In a small proportion of patients, a larger volume of 100 mL was administered based on clinical judgment. Dextrose was not administered as a continuous intravenous infusion. Patients with a CBG level ≥ 70 mg/dL did not receive prehospital dextrose. This study was conducted in accordance with the Standards for the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines for the reporting of observational studies18.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: This study included adult nontraumatic patients with OHCA aged ≥ 18 years who were dispatched to V-EMS, coded with Thailand emergency medical triage protocol and criteria-based dispatch symptom group 6 (cardiac arrest), underwent CBG testing during CPR, and delivered to the emergency department, Faculty of Medicine Vajira Hospital, Navamindradhiraj University, Bangkok, Thailand, between January 1, 2019, and June 30, 2023. Patients with death at the scene, those with signs of irreversible death concluded by team leaders as inappropriate to resuscitate, those with a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order, those with first-degree relatives denying resuscitation, those who underwent CPR during transfer, those with incomplete data, or those without resuscitation records were excluded from this study. Patients were divided into two groups: the dextrose group, which included patients with hypoglycemia who received dextrose during CPR, and the nondextrose group, which included patients with a CBG level of > 70 mg/dL who did not receive dextrose during CPR.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Data on patients with OHCA were collected from EMS patient care reports, a standard form used for recording advanced EMS operations performed by the Bangkok EMS (Erawan Center) and the Bangkok Advanced Emergency Operation Unit. This form comprised data on EMS operation units, patients, and all treatments of EMS teams, recorded by dispatchers and paramedics or ENPs operating at the scene. These data were part of the remuneration for the EMS operation units. Data on survival to hospital discharge were collected from the electronic medical records of Vajira Hospital. All data, including general characteristics of patients with OHCA (gender, age, underlying disease, location type, presumed cardiac arrest (a standard variable in EMS patient care reports for OHCA, where the cause of arrest is categorized into presumed cardiac arrest and other), CBG values were documented as categorical variables (≥ 70 mg/dL or < 70 mg/dL) to indicate the presence of hypoglycemia requiring dextrose administration, witnessed collapse, bystander CPR performed, initial rhythm, defibrillation, advanced airway management, prehospital fluid access, medication use during CPR process, total CPR time, time from CPR to dextrose administration, and dextrose amount) and study outcomes (sustained ROSC at the scene and survival-to-discharge), were collected and recorded in Microsoft Excel. Treatment outcomes were monitored every 30 days using EMS patient care reports and hospital electronic medical records abstracted by trained research assistants. The principal investigator oversaw data completeness and quality but was not involved in patient care and remained blinded to treatment allocation. Inpatient outcomes were monitored through electronic medical records of the Faculty of Medicine Vajira Hospital.

sec.title: Definitions
sec.p: Sustained ROSC at the scene is defined as a return of spontaneous circulation, characterized by a palpable pulse and measurable blood pressure at the scene, which are maintained for > 20 min16. Thirty-day survival is defined as the patient’s survival status at 30 days after the onset of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest16. Hypoglycemia is defined as a CBG level ≤ 70 mg/dL14,15 measured from a fingertip by EMS teams.

sec.title: Sample size
sec.p: The sample size was calculated using the formula for testing two independent proportions19. A significance level of 0.05 (α = 0.05) and a power of 90% were assumed. The statistical values used in the sample size calculation were obtained from a pilot study with retrospective data for 6 months from January 1, 2023, to June 30, 2023. The ratio of sustained ROSC at the scene between groups with and without dextrose administration during CPR was 56.67% (p1 = 0.5667; 17/30) and 34.48% (p2 = 0.3448; 10/29), respectively. A sample size ratio of 1:1 was determined based on the proportion of the retrospective population in the studied population. The simple size calculated using the formula was at least 104 for each group, totaling 208. To account for potential incomplete data, an additional 15% was added to the calculated sample size, resulting in a minimum sample size of 246 patients. Simple random sampling was performed.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Propensity scores were used to control for confounding factors that might influence dextrose administration during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Variables included in the propensity score model were selected a priori based on clinical relevance and evidence from prior literature, focusing on factors that could affect both the likelihood of receiving dextrose and patient outcomes. These variables included demographic characteristics, pre-arrest conditions, arrest characteristics, and prehospital resuscitation interventions measured before or during the early phase of resuscitation. Covariate balance between groups was assessed using standardized differences (STD), with an STD < 0.1 considered indicative of adequate balance. Variables with an STD > 0.1 after weighting were further adjusted for in multivariable analyses to account for residual confounding.

Univariable analyses were initially performed to assess crude associations between dextrose administration and study outcomes, including sustained return of spontaneous circulation at the scene and 30-day survival. Multivariable analyses were then conducted using logistic regression models to adjust for potential confounders. In addition, propensity score weighting with inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to estimate adjusted treatment effects. Results were reported as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 17.0 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). A p-value ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: General and clinical characteristics
sec.p: A total of 246 OHCA patients met the eligibility criteria, with 121 in the dextrose group and 125 in the nondextrose group (Fig. 1). Several baseline differences were observed between groups, including gender, location, cause of arrest, defibrillation, airway management, prehospital fluid use, and some medications (p < 0.05). IPTW was applied to balance these factors, and variables with standardized differences > 0.1 were further adjusted in multivariate analyses (Table 1; Fig. 2a and b).

sec.title: Subgroup characteristics by diabetes status
sec.p: Among diabetic patients (n = 53), those receiving dextrose were younger and more often managed outside public locations, with differences in airway techniques and fluid use (Table 2). Among nondiabetic patients (n = 193), baseline differences were also seen in gender, location, cause of arrest, fluid, and medication use (Table 3).

sec.title: Sustained ROSC at the scene
sec.p: Overall, sustained ROSC at the scene occurred in 45.5% of the dextrose group vs. 44.0% of the nondextrose group. After IPTW adjustment, dextrose administration was not significantly associated with sustained ROSC at the scene (adjusted RR = 1.13, 95% CI: 0.80–1.59, p = 0.484). In subgroup analysis, diabetic patients who received dextrose had a higher rate of sustained ROSC at the scene (50.0% vs. 45.2%) with borderline significance (adjusted RD = 26.01, p = 0.047), whereas no difference was seen in nondiabetics (Table 4; Fig. 3a and b).

sec.title: Survival to hospital discharge
sec.p: Overall survival to discharge was 25.6% in the dextrose group vs. 12.8% in the nondextrose group. After IPTW adjustment, dextrose administration significantly improved survival (adjusted RR = 2.38, 95% CI: 1.18–4.80, p = 0.015). The strongest effect was observed in diabetic patients (36.4% vs. 6.5%; adjusted RR = 18.86, p < 0.001). In nondiabetic patients, survival was higher in the dextrose group (23.2% vs. 14.9%), though not statistically significant (adjusted RR = 1.81, p = 0.084) (Table 4; Fig. 4a and b).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study demonstrated that intravenous dextrose administration during CPR in OHCA patients with hypoglycemia was not associated with improved sustained ROSC at the scene. However, dextrose administration was associated with better survival to hospital discharge, with the greatest benefit observed among patients with diabetes.

One possible explanation for the lack of improved ROSC is that hypoglycemia in OHCA may often be a consequence of the arrest rather than its cause. In such cases, correcting blood glucose alone would not address the underlying pathophysiology of ischemia, reperfusion injury, and multi-organ dysfunction. Furthermore, rapid fluctuations in glucose during resuscitation may contribute to metabolic instability, potentially offsetting the benefit of dextrose. These mechanisms may explain why improved survival to hospital discharge was observed in specific subgroups, while no significant effect was seen on immediate ROSC. Interestingly, nearly half of the patients in this study had blood glucose levels below 70 mg/dL, which is higher than typically reported in OHCA cohorts. This may reflect local population characteristics, particularly older age and a high prevalence of diabetes. These factors may limit the generalizability of our findings and should be considered when applying the results to other settings. The relationship between intra-arrest hypoglycemia and ROSC remains uncertain, with prior studies reporting inconsistent results, and robust evidence in the prehospital setting is still lacking10.

These findings indicate that EMS can postpone CBG testing until patients have ROSC because dextrose administration for treating hypoglycemia during cardiac arrest at the scene is not associated with the improvement of ROSC at the scene. These findings are consistent with the AHA standard guidelines in 201520, and 202013 which did not specify hypoglycemia as a reversible cause of cardiac arrest that should be treated during CPR because data showing that treating hypoglycemia can help improve outcomes were not clear enough. Therefore, these standard guidelines focused on continuous high-quality CPR, particularly efficient chest compression, to maintain a constant high level of chest compression fraction. Sufficient ventilation assistance and oxygen administration may provide better outcomes21 than blood glucose testing or IV dextrose administration, particularly in contexts with limited resources, such as prehospital OHCA care22. Although CBG testing is a simple test in prehospital contexts, high-quality CPR should not be interrupted.

Blood glucose testing should be a routine practice, especially in patients at risk of hypoglycemia, which can lead to cardiac arrest in some cases. Despite its rarity, blood glucose testing is important for patients with diabetes who usually use medications, particularly insulin or sulfonylurea, which can cause severe hypoglycemia if overdosed, those who do not eat after the medication administration, or those who have chronic malnutrition, especially in older adults or patients with chronic diseases with very high risk23,24. Additionally, patients with liver or renal failure have an increased risk because the liver and kidney have an essential role in controlling glucose level and related drug excretion25, and patients with a history of chronic alcoholism may experience impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis, particularly when fasting, leading to severe hypoglycemia26. Genetic abnormalities, such as glycogen storage disease, fatty acid oxidation disorders, and insulinoma, are also important causes27. When an EMS team is performing CPR, the CPR commander should be aware that those with the aforementioned risk factors may experience intracardiac arrest from severe hypoglycemia, which can cause cardiac dysrhythmia, seizure, unconsciousness, and finally cardiac arrest, particularly when glucose levels in the brain and cardiac muscle decrease so much that they cannot function normally23,28. The pathophysiological explanation is that the myocardial cells in humans receive most of their energy (> 60%–70%) from fatty acids as the main source of energy via β-oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation and a very small portion (approximately 5%) from glycolysis and glucose. Thus, blood sugar levels may not be a crucial factor for ROSC in patients experiencing a sudden cardiac arrest29.

A previous study found that IV access, which is required for IV dextrose administration, is a long procedure. Prehospital IV access takes almost 2 min or longer if the performer is a novice or inexperienced or performs other procedures at the same time, such as CPR, intubation, and defibrillation30. However, these problems can be resolved with regular practice and good teamwork. This study provides a novel finding that may contribute to modifying guidelines on OHCA patient care with severe hypoglycemia. This study provides new evidence that IV dextrose administration by EMS during CPR in patients with severe hypoglycemia can help raise survival to hospital discharge in all patients, particularly those with diabetes. These findings are consistent with those of a retrospective study, which showed that controlling and treating hypoglycemia during cardiac arrest was associated with improved survival rates and neurological outcomes at hospital discharge31. However, these findings conflict with those of an in-hospital cardiac arrest patient study, which showed that dextrose administration during CPR was associated with a significantly reduced chance of survival to hospital discharge and a decreased chance of good neurological outcome32. Additionally, they are inconsistent with those of a retrospective cohort study collecting in-hospital cardiac arrest patient data in Taiwan for 10 years, which reported that blood sugar level under 150 mg/dL and dextrose administration during CPR were associated with worsening neurological outcomes and survival to hospital discharge33. Therefore, our study results identified that CBG testing in patients with OHCA and dextrose administration by EMS teams during CPR could be used as indicators for predicting the outcomes of CPR and survival to hospital discharge. EMS personnel should ask additional targeted questions about the history of underlying diseases, such as diabetes, in patients with cardiac arrest to identify the causes of cardiac arrest.

This study showed that the organizational or regional standard guidelines on CPR should be followed, and CBG testing and dextrose administration should be considered. However, the direct association between dextrose administration and the outcome of survival-to-discharge may be limited because this study was not designed to investigate the effect of dextrose on survival to hospital discharge. It was not possible to discard the potential impact of unmeasurable or remaining confounding factors due to the observational nature of the study, particularly treatments in hospitals, and data on advanced invasive treatments in this patient group were lacking.

This study has some limitations. First, this was a retrospective cohort study using data from a single EMS center, which may restrict the generalizability of the results to other contexts. Second, because of the retrospective observational nature of the study, it was not possible to establish a causal relationship between CBG level and dextrose administration during CPR and patients’ outcomes. Even with strong statistical methods, such as propensity score analysis for reducing influences from confounding factors, unmeasured confounding factors might still exist, such as events before cardiac arrest, medication history, underlying diseases, and treatment in hospitals, especially advanced procedures, such as percutaneous coronary intervention and targeted temperature management, which were not included in this study. Third, there may be confounding variables that were not controlled for, such as the quality of CPR, types of diabetes, and nutritional status before cardiac arrest, which could affect the interpretation of the study results. An important limitation of this study relates to the comparison strategy dictated by real-world prehospital practice. According to the local EMS advanced life support protocol, intravenous dextrose is routinely administered to all patients with documented hypoglycemia (CBG < 70 mg/dL) once intravenous access is successfully established during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Consequently, there were no patients with confirmed hypoglycemia who did not receive dextrose because of failed or delayed intravenous access, precluding a direct comparison between hypoglycemic patients who did and did not receive dextrose. As a result, the present study compared patients with hypoglycemia who received dextrose with patients without hypoglycemia who did not receive dextrose, using propensity score weighting to mitigate confounding. Nevertheless, residual confounding related to differences in underlying metabolic status and arrest characteristics cannot be fully excluded, and causal inference remains limited by the observational design. Future studies conducted in settings with greater variability in prehospital practice or multicenter datasets may allow for more direct comparisons and provide stronger evidence regarding the effectiveness of dextrose administration during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Fourth, patients in the dextrose group were included based on a CBG level of ≤ 70 mg/dL, whereas those in the nondextrose group were included based on a CBG level of > 70 mg/dL, which might limit the application of the results in contexts with different CBG cutoff points. Additionally, patients who did not undergo CBG testing during CPR were excluded from this study, which may have resulted in selection bias. Fifth, the nondextrose group was defined as those with a CBG level of > 70 mg/dL without a certain range. High blood sugar levels may be a factor that affects the results. However, we believe that the difference in sugar levels in this group should not be a direct cause of cardiac arrest. Sixth, the sample size was originally calculated for a two-group comparison (dextrose vs. non-dextrose). Subgroup analyses by diabetes status created four groups, for which no re-estimation of sample size was performed. Therefore, these subgroup analyses may have been underpowered to detect differences with the desired 90% power. Seventh, approximately 20% of initially eligible cases were excluded because of incomplete EMS or hospital records. Patterns of missing data were assessed by examining the frequency and distribution of missing variables across study groups and by evaluating their association with key baseline characteristics and primary outcomes. No clear systematic pattern of missingness related to treatment group allocation or outcomes was identified. Nevertheless, this exclusion may have introduced selection bias and limited the generalizability of the findings. Sensitivity analyses were not feasible in this retrospective dataset; therefore, future studies with more complete and standardized data collection are warranted to confirm the robustness of the results. Eighth, nearly half of the patients in this study had blood glucose levels below 70 mg/dL, which is higher than commonly reported in other OHCA cohorts. This may reflect local population characteristics, particularly older age and a high prevalence of diabetes. As a result, the generalizability of our findings to other populations may be limited. Ninth, CBG levels were recorded as categorical variables (< 70 mg/dL vs. ≥70 mg/dL), and continuous measurements were not available. This limited our ability to analyze dose–response effects or to report mean and median glucose levels. In addition, subgroup analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, and the possibility of type I (alpha) error cannot be excluded. These results should therefore be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Tenth, the study did not include data on in-hospital intravenous dextrose administration; therefore, we were unable to directly compare prehospital and in-hospital treatment among patients with OHCA and hypoglycemia. This limitation restricts the validity of the comparison and highlights the need for future studies with linked prehospital and in-hospital data to clarify the optimal timing of dextrose administration. Eleventh, CBG was documented only in categorical form (< 70 mg/dL vs. ≥70 mg/dL), which prevented us from distinguishing varying levels of hyperglycemia. Markedly elevated glucose, as observed in septic shock or diabetic ketoacidosis, could directly contribute to cardiac arrest. Therefore, our study could not assess the potential causal role of severe hyperglycemia, and future research with continuous glucose data is warranted. Finally, this study was limited to outcomes of sustained ROSC at the scene and survival to hospital discharge without investigating long-term outcomes, specifically neurological outcomes, due to the restriction of the electronic medical data record system in the study area. Therefore, further prospective studies with complete data collection are needed to address these limitations.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and hypoglycemia, prehospital intravenous dextrose administration during cardiopulmonary resuscitation was not associated with improved sustained return of spontaneous circulation at the scene but was associated with improved 30-day survival, particularly among patients with diabetes.
